title: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds: why salt shatters, wax melts and metal bends

summary.text: Press a crystal of salt with a spoon, and it cracks into pieces. Press a ball of aluminium foil, and it only flattens. Both are solids made of atoms that hold on to each other. They hold on in different ways. In salt, atoms give and take electrons, and become charged particles called ions. In water, wax and sugar, atoms share electrons and make molecules. In a metal, all the atoms share their outer electrons together. Your child presses, heats and wets three solids to tell the three kinds of bond apart. They also find out why dry salt does not carry electricity and wet salt does.
summary.art: A steel plate seen from above with a cracked salt crystal in several pieces on one side and a flattened disc of aluminium foil on the other, and a steel spoon between them.

intro.hook: Sodium is a soft metal that can catch fire in water. Chlorine is a poisonous green gas. Joined together, they are the salt in your sambar. How can joining change two things so much?
intro.text: A bond is the way atoms hold on to each other. The kind of bond decides how a material behaves. In this unit you press a salt crystal and a ball of foil, and see one break and one bend. You heat salt, wax and foil over a candle with a grown-up. You build a tester from a battery and two pencils. With it you find out when salt carries electricity. By the end you can say what happened to the sodium and the chlorine.
intro.art: A small heap of white table salt on a banana leaf beside a bowl of sambar, with a faint drawing above it of a grey lump of metal and a pale green cloud joined by an arrow to the salt.

outcomes: I can say what an ion is, and how an atom becomes one.
I can describe an ionic bond, and explain why salt is hard, brittle and hard to melt.
I can describe a covalent bond, and explain why wax and ice melt easily.
I can describe a metallic bond, and explain why metals bend, shine and carry electricity.
I can explain why salt carries electricity only when its ions are free to move.
I can use tests to work out how a solid is held together.
I can tell from the kinds of atoms which bond to expect, and work out a simple formula.
I can say how people found out that salt has no molecules, and what is still argued about bonds.

terms.meaning: A very tiny particle with a minus electric charge. Electrons move around the centre of every atom.
terms.example: The outer electrons of an atom are the ones that make bonds.
terms.art: A small centre marked plus with a few dots marked minus spread around it, and the outermost dots drawn in a brighter colour.

terms.meaning: The way atoms hold on to each other. Every bond comes from plus charges and minus charges attracting each other.
terms.example: Bonds hold the atoms of a salt crystal, a drop of water and a steel spoon together.
terms.art: Two round atoms close together with a glowing band between them.

terms.meaning: Metals are elements such as iron, copper, sodium and gold. Their atoms hold their outer electrons weakly. Non-metals are elements such as oxygen, chlorine and carbon. Their atoms hold electrons strongly.
terms.example: Sodium is a metal. Chlorine is a non-metal.
terms.art: Two groups of labelled circles: iron, copper, sodium and gold on the left, oxygen, chlorine and carbon on the right.

terms.meaning: An atom that has lost or gained electrons, so it has an electric charge. Losing electrons makes a plus ion. Gaining electrons makes a minus ion.
terms.example: A sodium atom that gives away one electron becomes a sodium ion with a plus charge.
terms.art: A circle marked Na with a plus sign beside a larger circle marked Cl with a minus sign.

terms.meaning: The attraction between plus ions and minus ions. It forms when metal atoms give electrons to non-metal atoms.
terms.example: Table salt is sodium ions and chloride ions held by ionic bonds.
terms.art: A small plus circle and a large minus circle with short lines of attraction drawn between them.

terms.meaning: A regular pattern of particles that repeats in every direction through a crystal.
terms.example: In a salt lattice, every sodium ion has six chloride ions around it.
terms.art: A cube built of small and large balls placed in turns, like a three-dimensional chessboard.

terms.meaning: A bond made when two atoms share a pair of electrons. It forms between non-metal atoms.
terms.example: In water, the oxygen atom shares electrons with two hydrogen atoms.
terms.art: Two overlapping circles with two dots drawn in the part where they overlap.

terms.meaning: A group of atoms joined by covalent bonds. It is the smallest piece of a substance such as water or sugar.
terms.example: A water molecule is one oxygen atom joined to two hydrogen atoms.
terms.art: One large ball with two small balls attached to it at an angle.

terms.meaning: The bond in a metal. All the atoms share their outer electrons, and these electrons move freely among them.
terms.example: In a copper wire, the free electrons are shared by every copper atom in the wire.
terms.art: Rows of identical circles marked plus, with many small dots scattered freely in the gaps between them.

terms.meaning: Breaking suddenly into pieces when pressed or hit, without bending first.
terms.example: A salt crystal and a piece of chalk are brittle.
terms.art: A crystal under the back of a spoon with crack lines running through it.

terms.meaning: Able to be pressed or beaten into a new shape without breaking.
terms.example: Silver is so malleable that it is beaten into the thin leaf put on sweets.
terms.art: A hammer above a metal lump that has spread into a thin flat sheet.

terms.meaning: A material that lets electricity pass through it.
terms.example: Copper, steel and salt water are conductors.
terms.art: A wire leading into a metal spoon and out again, with small arrows passing through the spoon.

terms.meaning: A material that does not let electricity pass through it.
terms.example: Candle wax, dry sugar and dry salt are insulators.
terms.art: A wire leading into a candle, with the small arrows stopping at the candle.

terms.meaning: A substance that carries electricity when it is dissolved or melted, because its ions can move.
terms.example: The salts in ORS are electrolytes.
terms.art: A glass of water with plus and minus dots drifting in opposite directions between two rods.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
terms.example: Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius. Salt melts at about 800 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A thermometer scale with an ice cube marked low down and a salt crystal marked far above it.

terms.meaning: A metal made by mixing a metal with one or more other elements.
terms.example: Steel is an alloy of iron. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
terms.art: A brass lamp, with a magnified circle showing two sizes of atoms mixed in neat rows.

explanations.definition: A chemical bond is the way atoms hold on to each other. Every bond comes from the attraction between plus charges and minus charges.
explanations.description: Every atom has a centre called the nucleus, which has a plus charge. Around it move electrons, which have a minus charge. Plus and minus attract each other. An electron is attracted to its own nucleus. If another atom comes close, the electron is attracted to that nucleus too. That double attraction is what holds atoms together. Only the outer electrons take part, because they are the furthest from their own nucleus. There are three main things the outer electrons can do. One atom can give electrons to another. That makes an ionic bond. Two atoms can share electrons between them. That makes a covalent bond. A whole crowd of atoms can share their electrons together. That makes a metallic bond. Salt, water and copper are held in these three ways.
examples: Salt is held by ionic bonds.
Water, wax and sugar are held by covalent bonds.
Copper, aluminium and steel are held by metallic bonds.
explanations.art: Three small panels: one atom handing a dot to another, two atoms with two dots between them, and a row of atoms with many dots loose among them.

explanations.concept: Ionic bonds: one atom gives, another takes
explanations.definition: An ion is an atom with an electric charge, because it has lost or gained electrons. An ionic bond is the attraction between plus ions and minus ions.
explanations.description: A sodium atom holds its one outer electron weakly. A chlorine atom attracts one more electron strongly. When they meet, the electron moves from the sodium to the chlorine. The sodium now has one electron too few, so it has a plus charge. The chlorine has one too many, so it has a minus charge. Both are now ions. The chlorine ion is called chloride. A sodium ion is not like a sodium atom. The atom reacts fiercely because it gives its electron away so easily. The ion has already given it away, so it does not react in that way. This is how a fiery metal and a poisonous gas become table salt. The ions do not pair off. Each plus ion attracts every minus ion near it. So they pack into a pattern called a lattice, plus next to minus in every direction. In salt, every sodium ion has six chloride ions around it. Every chloride ion has six sodium ions around it. There is no salt molecule. The formula NaCl only says there is one sodium ion for every chloride ion.
examples: Table salt is sodium ions and chloride ions.
Cooking soda has sodium ions, and toothpaste often has sodium fluoride.
A sea shell is mostly calcium carbonate, which is held together by ionic bonds.
explanations.art: A cube of small and large balls placed in turns, with one small ball in the middle picked out and lines drawn to its six nearest large neighbours.

explanations.concept: Why salt is hard, brittle and hard to melt
explanations.context: This card explains the experiment Three Solids, Three Tests. In it, salt cracked when pressed and stayed solid over a candle flame.
explanations.definition: An ionic solid is hard and brittle, and it melts only at a very high temperature. This is because every ion is held by strong attractions on all sides.
explanations.description: In Three Solids, Three Tests, the salt cracked under the spoon. It did not melt over the candle, and it dissolved in water. To melt salt, the ions must break free of all their neighbours. That needs about 800 degrees Celsius. A candle flame warms a spoon to a few hundred degrees at most. Salt is hard for the same reason. It is brittle because of the pattern. Press hard, and one layer of ions slips one place sideways. Now plus ions sit next to plus ions, and minus next to minus. Like charges repel each other. So the two layers push apart, and the crystal splits along a flat face. Water takes salt apart more gently. Water molecules attract the ions and pull them out of the lattice one by one.
examples: A crystal of rock salt breaks into pieces with flat faces.
Salt stays solid on a hot dosa tawa.
Factories melt salt and pass electricity through it to make sodium metal.
explanations.art: Two drawings of a checkerboard of plus and minus circles: one in order, and one with the top half slid one place so that like signs face each other along a crack.

explanations.definition: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared by two atoms. Atoms joined by covalent bonds make a molecule.
explanations.description: Non-metal atoms all attract electrons strongly, so neither atom can take an electron from the other. They share. In a water molecule, the oxygen atom shares a pair of electrons with each of two hydrogen atoms. The shared pair is attracted by both atoms, and that holds them together. Covalent bonds inside a molecule are very strong. But one molecule attracts the next molecule only weakly. Melting does not break any covalent bonds. It only lets whole molecules slide past each other. So most substances made of molecules melt easily. Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius, and candle wax at about 60. In Three Solids, Three Tests, the wax melted within seconds. Molecules have no charge, and their electrons stay in their bonds. So wax and sugar do not carry electricity. A few covalent solids are not made of small molecules. In a diamond, every carbon atom is bonded to four others, all through the stone. To break or melt a diamond, covalent bonds themselves must break. That is why diamond is the hardest natural material.
examples: Water, sugar, cooking oil, wax and plastic are made of covalent molecules.
The oxygen and nitrogen in air are molecules of two atoms each.
Diamond and the quartz in sand are covalent all the way through.
explanations.art: A water molecule drawn as one large ball and two small balls, with two dots in each place where the balls overlap, beside a candle with a magnified circle showing long chain molecules lying side by side.

explanations.concept: Metallic bonds: all the atoms share
explanations.definition: In a metallic bond, every atom gives its outer electrons to a pool shared by the whole piece of metal. The electrons move freely, and they hold all the atoms together.
explanations.description: Metal atoms hold their outer electrons weakly. In a piece of metal, these electrons leave their own atoms. They move freely among all the atoms. What is left of each atom has a plus charge. The plus atoms are held together by the minus electrons moving between them. This explains what metals do. A metal bends because its atoms can slide to new places and the electrons still hold them. So a ball of foil flattens and a paper clip bends. A metal carries electricity because its free electrons can flow along it. A metal shines because the free electrons send light back from its surface. Free electrons carry heat too, so a steel spoon in hot rasam soon feels hot. Metals melt at very different temperatures. Mercury is a liquid at room temperature. Aluminium melts at 660 degrees Celsius, and iron at about 1,540. An alloy is a metal mixed with other elements. Atoms of a different size make it harder for the layers to slide. So steel is harder than pure iron.
examples: Gold is beaten into leaf only a few hundred atoms thick.
Copper is pulled into wire for every house.
Bronze idols and bell-metal urulis are alloys of copper and tin.
explanations.art: Rows of identical plus circles with many small dots between them, drawn twice: once in a straight block and once with the top rows slid sideways, with the dots still filling every gap.

explanations.concept: When salt carries electricity, and when it does not
explanations.context: This card explains the experiment Dry Salt, Wet Salt. In it, dry salt carried no electricity, and the same salt carried it when wet.
explanations.definition: Electricity passes through a material only if it has charged particles that are free to move. In a metal these are electrons. In salt water they are ions.
explanations.description: In Dry Salt, Wet Salt, the steel spoon carried electricity and the candle did not. Dry salt did not carry it. Wet salt did. Dry salt is full of charged ions, but each one is held in place by its neighbours. Charges that cannot move cannot carry electricity. Water pulls the ions out of the lattice. Now they can drift through the water. The plus sodium ions drift towards the minus wire. The minus chloride ions drift towards the plus wire. That moving charge is the current. Sugar dissolves as whole molecules with no charge, so sugar water carries hardly any electricity. Pure water carries hardly any either. Tap water carries a little, because it always has some salts dissolved in it. Melting frees ions too. In 1807 Humphry Davy melted a white solid called potash and passed electricity through it. Shining drops of a new metal, potassium, appeared. A substance that carries electricity through its moving ions is called an electrolyte. Your nerves and muscles work by moving sodium and potassium ions through water.
examples: Salt water carries electricity, and dry salt does not.
ORS puts back the electrolytes that a sick child loses.
The liquid inside a phone battery carries lithium ions from one side to the other.
explanations.art: Two plates side by side: a dry heap of salt with two wires in it and no arrows, and a wet heap with plus and minus dots drifting in opposite directions between the wires.

explanations.concept: Which bond is it? The kinds of atoms, and four tests
explanations.definition: The kinds of atoms in a substance tell you which bond to expect. Tests then check it.
explanations.description: Start with the atoms. Metal atoms with non-metal atoms usually make ionic bonds. Non-metal atoms alone make covalent bonds. Metal atoms alone make metallic bonds. Then test. An ionic solid is brittle, and it does not melt on a kitchen flame. It often dissolves in water, and then the water carries electricity. A solid made of covalent molecules is soft or brittle, and it melts easily. It does not carry electricity, dry or dissolved. A metal bends or flattens, and it carries electricity as a dry solid. No single test is enough. Sugar is brittle like salt, and it dissolves like salt. Only the electricity test tells them apart. There are exceptions. Pencil lead is graphite, which is covalent, yet it carries electricity. Each carbon atom in graphite has one electron that is free to move. Lemon juice and vinegar are made of covalent molecules. In water some of these molecules split into ions, so they carry some electricity.
examples: Sodium fluoride is a metal with a non-metal, so it is ionic.
Carbon dioxide is two non-metals, so it is covalent.
Brass is copper and zinc, two metals, so it is metallic.
explanations.art: A table with three rows labelled ionic, covalent molecules and metallic, and four columns of small pictures: a spoon pressing, a candle, a glass of water and a battery.

explanations.concept: Why water dissolves salt but not wax
explanations.definition: The electrons in a water molecule are not shared equally. This gives each water molecule a slightly minus end and a slightly plus end, which attract ions.
explanations.description: In a water molecule, the oxygen atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly than the hydrogen atoms do. So the electrons spend more time near the oxygen. The oxygen end of the molecule is slightly minus. The hydrogen ends are slightly plus. When salt meets water, the oxygen ends turn towards the plus sodium ions. The hydrogen ends turn towards the minus chloride ions. Many water molecules together attract an ion more strongly than the lattice holds it. The ion comes away with a coat of water molecules around it. Wax molecules share their electrons almost equally, so they have no charged ends. Water molecules attract each other far more than they attract wax. So wax stays out of the water. In Three Solids, Three Tests, the salt dissolved and the wax floated unchanged.
examples: Salt and sugar dissolve in water.
Oil, ghee and wax do not dissolve in water.
Water runs off a waxy lotus leaf in round drops.
explanations.art: A sodium ion surrounded by water molecules with their oxygen ends turned towards it, and a chloride ion surrounded by water molecules with their hydrogen ends turned towards it.

explanations.concept: Most real bonds are a mixture
explanations.definition: Ionic, covalent and metallic are three pure types. Most real bonds lie somewhere between them.
explanations.description: In 1932 the American chemist Linus Pauling gave each element a number. The number says how strongly its atoms attract shared electrons. If two atoms have the same number, they share equally. That is a pure covalent bond, as in oxygen gas. If the numbers differ a little, the sharing is unequal, as in water. If they differ a lot, one atom takes the electron almost fully, as in salt. So there is no sharp line between sharing and giving. Even in salt, the electron is not given completely. Later chemists drew a triangle with the three pure types at its corners. Salt sits near the ionic corner, and copper near the metallic corner. Most substances sit somewhere inside the triangle.
examples: Oxygen gas is shared equally.
Water is shared unequally.
Salt is almost fully given.
explanations.art: A triangle with the words ionic, covalent and metallic at its corners, and dots labelled salt, water, oxygen gas, copper and graphite placed at different spots inside it.

explanations.concept: Bonds can change under pressure: hydrogen inside Jupiter
explanations.definition: Hydrogen on Earth is a gas of covalent molecules. Scientists think that deep inside Jupiter, it is squeezed into a liquid metal.
explanations.description: The kind of bond is not fixed for ever by the kind of atom. It also depends on how hard the atoms are pressed together. In 1935 Eugene Wigner and Hillard Huntington worked out that hydrogen should become a metal under great pressure. The atoms would be pushed so close that their electrons would be shared by all. In 1996 a team in California squeezed liquid hydrogen with a shock for a tiny moment. It carried electricity like a metal. Deep inside Jupiter the pressure is millions of times greater than our air pressure. Scientists think most of Jupiter's hydrogen is a liquid metal. Currents in it would explain Jupiter's very strong magnetism. Nobody has been there to check. In 2017 two scientists at Harvard reported solid metallic hydrogen made in a laboratory. Other teams have not been able to repeat it.
examples: Hydrogen gas in a balloon is made of molecules of two atoms.
Jupiter's magnetism is the strongest of any planet.
Earth's own magnetism comes from liquid iron moving in its core.
explanations.art: A cutaway of Jupiter showing a thin outer layer of gas and a deep inner layer drawn as a sea of dots, with a small diagram of two-atom molecules above and a pool of shared electrons below.

explanations.definition: Chemists draw a bond as a line between two atoms. They disagree about whether that line stands for a real object.
explanations.description: Nobody has picked up a bond. What exists for certain is nuclei and electrons. A bond is where electrons gather between nuclei and lower the energy. Whether to call that a thing is argued.
examples: A chemist draws water as H, a line, O, a line, H.
In 2009 a microscope picture of a molecule showed bright lines where chemists draw bonds.

perspectives.explanation: Bonds are real. They have a length and a strength that can be measured. In 2009 Leo Gross and his team in Zurich pictured a single molecule with a very fine microscope. The picture showed lines where the bonds were drawn.

perspectives.who: Some chemists and physicists who work with quantum theory
perspectives.explanation: Only nuclei and electrons are real. The electrons spread through the whole molecule as a cloud. A bond is our name for one part of that cloud. The lines in the picture show where electrons are thick, which fits both views.

explanations.art: A chemist's stick drawing of a molecule beside a blurry microscope picture of the same molecule with faint lines in the same places.

agreed.text: Salt has no molecules. Its ions sit in turns in a lattice, and each has six neighbours of the other kind.
agreed.evidence: In 1913 Lawrence Bragg worked this out from the pattern that X-rays make when they pass through a salt crystal. Every later measurement has agreed.

agreed.text: Melted or dissolved salts carry electricity, because their ions move.
agreed.evidence: In 1807 Humphry Davy passed electricity through melted potash and got potassium metal. In 1834 Michael Faraday named the moving particles ions. In 1884 Svante Arrhenius showed that the ions are already present in salt water before any current flows.

agreed.text: The electricity in a metal is carried by electrons that are free to move.
agreed.evidence: In 1916 Richard Tolman and Dale Stewart spun a coil of wire very fast and stopped it suddenly. A brief current flowed, because the free electrons kept moving for a moment. Its direction showed the moving charges were minus.

agreed.text: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared by two atoms.
agreed.evidence: Gilbert Lewis proposed this in 1916. In 1927 Walter Heitler and Fritz London calculated the bond in a hydrogen molecule from quantum theory. Their answer came close to the measured strength.

agreed.text: Covalent bonds hold atoms at fixed distances and angles.
agreed.evidence: In 1929 Kathleen Lonsdale used X-rays to show that a ring of six carbon atoms is flat. She measured the distances between the atoms. Dorothy Hodgkin later mapped penicillin and insulin atom by atom in the same way.

agreed.text: There is no sharp line between sharing an electron and giving it.
agreed.evidence: In 1932 Linus Pauling measured bond strengths and gave each element a number for how strongly it attracts electrons. Bonds between elements with different numbers come out part shared and part given.

challenging.claim: Salt is made of salt molecules, each with one sodium atom and one chlorine atom.
challenging.who: Most chemists before 1913, and Henry Armstrong as late as 1927.
challenging.for: The formula NaCl looks like a molecule. Water and sugar really are made of molecules.
challenging.against: X-rays show that each ion has six equal neighbours and no partner of its own. NaCl gives only the ratio, one to one.

challenging.claim: Salt water has no ions until an electric current makes them.
challenging.who: Michael Faraday and most chemists before 1884.
challenging.for: Ions were first noticed only when a current was flowing.
challenging.against: Svante Arrhenius showed in 1884 that dissolved salt is already split into ions. Salt lowers the freezing point of water about twice as much as the same number of sugar molecules. That fits two particles for every unit of salt.

challenging.for: People get electric shocks with wet hands, so water seems to carry electricity.
challenging.against: Pure water carries very little. The salts dissolved in tap water, sweat and sea water carry it. Since nearly all water around us has salts, wet hands near a socket are truly dangerous.

challenging.claim: Ionic, covalent and metallic are three separate kinds of bond.
challenging.for: The three types explain the tests in this unit well.
challenging.against: Linus Pauling showed in 1932 that sharing shades into giving with no sharp line. Graphite is covalent and still carries electricity. The three types are corners, and most bonds lie between them.

challenging.claim: Every atom bonds until it has eight outer electrons.
challenging.who: A rule of thumb from Gilbert Lewis and Irving Langmuir, used in most school books.
challenging.for: The rule gives the right formula for salt, water and many other compounds.
challenging.against: Hydrogen stops at two. Many atoms, such as sulphur and iron, often break the rule. Chemists use it as a quick guide and check it against measurements.

challenging.claim: Hydrogen, the lightest gas, becomes a metal if it is squeezed hard enough.
challenging.who: Eugene Wigner and Hillard Huntington in 1935.
challenging.for: Liquid hydrogen squeezed by a shock carried electricity like a metal in 1996. Jupiter's strong magnetism fits a deep layer of metallic hydrogen.
challenging.against: Solid metallic hydrogen was reported in 2017, but no other team has repeated it. The pressure needed is very hard to reach and to measure.

big_questions.q: Sodium metal burns in water, and the sodium ions in salt do not. Are they the same thing?
big_questions.hint: The nucleus is the same. Only one electron is missing. What makes a thing what it is?

big_questions.q: Dry salt does not carry electricity, and wet salt does. Is carrying electricity a fact about salt, or about salt and water together?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you found in Dry Salt, Wet Salt. Could you call salt a conductor, an insulator, or neither?

big_questions.q: In a copper wire, the free electrons belong to no single atom. Is the wire many atoms, or one thing?
big_questions.hint: A salt crystal has no pairs either. Where would you draw the edge of one piece?

big_questions.q: Nobody has picked up a bond. Is a bond a thing, or a name for what electrons do?
big_questions.hint: A wave on the sea can be seen and measured. Is a wave a thing?

big_questions.q: Your nerves send messages by moving ions through water. Where did the ions in your body come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about salt, food, the sea and the rocks that rivers wear down.

big_questions.q: Lawrence Bragg was 23, and a famous older chemist called his idea absurd. How should people decide whom to trust?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each of them could show, and whether other people could repeat it.

story.title: The Bell That Sang at Dawn
story.note: Poongodi, Aachi, Kathir and Mumtaz are made up. These facts are real. Vedaranyam is a town on the coast of Tamil Nadu where people have made salt from sea water for centuries. Sea wind leaves a thin crust of salt on things near the shore. Sea salt takes in water from damp air. A musical doorbell starts playing when a very small current passes between the two contacts of its button. Such bells often ring by themselves in rain or mist. Electricity companies near the sea wash salt off their power lines for the same reason.
text: The bell sang at ten to six in the morning, and nobody was at the gate.

Poongodi heard it from her mat. It was the new bell that her aunt had brought from Nagapattinam. It ran on two pencil cells, and it played a tune like a film song. Its button was screwed to the gatepost, facing the sea road.
Aachi was already up. She was drawing the Margazhi kolam by the front step. She looked at the empty gate, and went on drawing.
"That is the third morning," said Poongodi.
"It is the sea," said Aachi. "She was ringing bells here before there were bells."
Aachi had worked for forty years in the salt pans of Vedaranyam. She said things like that, and she did not explain them. Poongodi was nine, and she liked things explained.

So she kept watch. At noon the gatepost was hot and dry, and the bell was silent. Her little cousin Kathir pressed the button, and it sang. He let go, and it stopped. Nothing was wrong with the bell. At four it was silent. At night she fell asleep still listening.
At ten to six the next morning it sang again. This time Poongodi reached the gate before the tune ended.

Nobody was there. A thick white mist lay over the road. She could not see the neem tree on the far side. The gatepost was wet, as if someone had washed it. She put her finger on the wet wood, and then on her tongue.
It tasted of salt.

She looked closely at the button. Its plastic cover had a crack across it. Around the crack, and over the two small screws, lay a thin white crust. She knew that crust. It was on the window bars and on the cycle. It was on Aachi's spectacles every evening. The sea wind carried salt in, and left it on everything.
"It is the salt," she told Aachi. "The salt joins the two screws, just as the button does."
"The salt is there at noon also," said Aachi. She did not look up from her kolam. "At noon your bell is quiet."
That was true, and it was annoying. The crust sat on the button all day long. The bell sang only at dawn.

Poongodi thought about it through breakfast. She thought about the wet gatepost. She thought about Aachi's salt, which lay in dry white heaps beside the pans. Aachi always said that a heap was finished, and the wet pan was still at work.
At noon she went back to the gate with Kathir. The crust was dry and bright in the sun. The bell was silent.
"Watch," she said. She put her mouth close to the button, as she did to clean her spectacles. She breathed out, long and slow. "Haaaa."
For a moment nothing happened. Then the bell began to sing.
Kathir jumped. "You did not touch it!"
"I only made it wet." The tune ran on. Then the sun dried the crust, and the tune stopped in the middle.
She dipped one finger in the water pot and let a single drop fall on the crack. The bell sang again. This time it would not stop until Kathir wiped the button with his shirt.
"Dry salt sits still," said Poongodi slowly. "Wet salt lets the bell's electricity cross. The mist comes at dawn and wets the crust. That is all."
Aachi had come to the gate with her kolam powder still on her fingers. "So I was wrong?" she asked.
Poongodi thought about it. "No. The sea sends the salt, and the sea sends the mist. It is the sea. You only left out the middle."
Aachi laughed until she had to hold the gatepost.

They mended it together. Poongodi took the two cells out first. Aachi poured drinking water over the button until no white was left. They let it dry in the sun for an hour. Then Poongodi lit the stub of a candle and let the wax drip over the crack and over both screws. The wax set hard and smooth.
"Why wax?" asked Kathir.
"Water runs off wax. And wax lets nothing cross it, wet or dry."
The next dawn the mist came in as thick as before. The gatepost dripped. Poongodi lay on her mat with her eyes open, and the bell did not sing.
At half past six it sang.
She ran to the gate. Mumtaz, who sold fish from a basket on her head, stood there with her thumb on the button.
"Your bell works," said Mumtaz.
"Now it does," said Poongodi. "Now it only sings for people."
story.epiphany: The salt crust lay on the button all day, but the bell sang only when the mist wetted it. Dry salt does not carry electricity, because its charged ions are held in place. Wet salt carries it, because the ions can move through the water.
ask: The salt crust was on the button at noon and at dawn. What was different at dawn?
A drop of water on a salt crust lets electricity cross. What do you think the water does to the salt?
Why did candle wax keep the bell quiet in the mist, when salt did not?
