games.title: Give, Share or Pool? A bond sorting card game
games.context: This is a card game about the three kinds of bond. Each card names a material and the kinds of atoms in it. You decide if its atoms give, share or pool their electrons.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile on a table, with three small tokens marked Ionic, Covalent and Metallic in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while another player slides one token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down one token, face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 24 material cards: the material and its atoms on the front, the bond and the reason on the back

items.f: Table salt. It is made of sodium, a metal, and chlorine, a non-metal.
items.b: Ionic. Sodium atoms give electrons to chlorine atoms. The ions attract each other.

items.f: Cooking soda. It has sodium, a metal, with hydrogen, carbon and oxygen, which are non-metals.
items.b: Ionic. Sodium ions are held to minus ions made of hydrogen, carbon and oxygen.

items.f: Quicklime, used to make whitewash. It is calcium, a metal, and oxygen, a non-metal.
items.b: Ionic. Each calcium atom gives two electrons to an oxygen atom.

items.f: The fluoride in toothpaste. It is sodium, a metal, and fluorine, a non-metal.
items.b: Ionic. Sodium fluoride is sodium ions and fluoride ions.

items.f: Potassium chloride in an ORS packet. Potassium is a metal, and chlorine is a non-metal.
items.b: Ionic. In water its ions move apart, so it is an electrolyte.

items.f: A ruby. It is mostly aluminium, a metal, and oxygen, a non-metal.
items.b: Ionic. Strong attractions between the ions make a ruby very hard.

items.f: A sea shell. It is calcium, a metal, with carbon and oxygen, which are non-metals.
items.b: Ionic. Calcium ions are held to minus ions made of carbon and oxygen.

items.f: The magnesium chloride in sea salt. Magnesium is a metal, and chlorine is a non-metal.
items.b: Ionic. Each magnesium atom gives one electron to each of two chlorine atoms.

items.f: Water. It is hydrogen and oxygen, two non-metals.
items.b: Covalent. The oxygen atom shares electrons with two hydrogen atoms.

items.f: Sugar. It is carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, three non-metals.
items.b: Covalent. Sugar is made of molecules, and they have no charge.

items.f: Candle wax. It is carbon and hydrogen, two non-metals.
items.b: Covalent. Wax molecules are long chains that hold each other weakly, so wax melts easily.

items.f: Cooking gas. It is carbon and hydrogen, two non-metals.
items.b: Covalent. Its small molecules hold each other so weakly that it is a gas.

items.f: The oxygen in air. It is oxygen atoms only, a non-metal.
items.b: Covalent. Two oxygen atoms share electrons equally and make one molecule.

items.f: Carbon dioxide in your breath. It is carbon and oxygen, two non-metals.
items.b: Covalent. One carbon atom shares electrons with two oxygen atoms.

items.f: A diamond. It is carbon atoms only, a non-metal.
items.b: Covalent. Every carbon atom shares electrons with four others, all through the stone.

items.f: A plastic bottle. It is carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, three non-metals.
items.b: Covalent. Plastic is made of very long chain molecules.

items.f: Copper wire. It is copper atoms only, a metal.
items.b: Metallic. The free electrons carry electricity along the wire.

items.f: Aluminium foil. It is aluminium atoms only, a metal.
items.b: Metallic. The atoms slide and still hold, so it can be rolled very thin.

items.f: A gold bangle. It is gold mixed with a little copper, both metals.
items.b: Metallic. It is an alloy, and all its atoms share their outer electrons.

items.f: A steel spoon. It is mostly iron and chromium, both metals.
items.b: Metallic. Steel is an alloy of iron.

items.f: Silver leaf on a sweet. It is silver atoms only, a metal.
items.b: Metallic. Silver can be beaten very thin because its atoms slide and still hold.

items.f: A brass lamp. It is copper and zinc, both metals.
items.b: Metallic. Brass is an alloy of two metals.

items.f: A bell-metal uruli. It is copper and tin, both metals.
items.b: Metallic. Bell metal is an alloy that rings when struck.

items.f: The mercury in an old thermometer. It is mercury atoms only, a metal.
items.b: Metallic. Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature.

printables.title: 3 bond tokens: Ionic, Covalent, Metallic. Print one set for each player
items: Ionic: a metal gives electrons to a non-metal
Metallic: metal atoms pool their electrons

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one bond token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the bond on the back scores 1 point.
A player who also says one thing the material will do scores 1 more point. It may bend, shatter, melt easily or carry electricity.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say the bond aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right bond.
After all 24 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 24 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of three tokens.
flow.say: Each card names a material and the kinds of atoms in it. Your three tokens are the three kinds of bond. Here is the guide. A metal with a non-metal gives. Non-metals share. Metals alone pool.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Give, Share or Pool. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first twelve cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card six.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a bond token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide which bond the card describes?
good: I looked at whether the atoms were metals or non-metals.
A metal with a non-metal is ionic.
Only metals means metallic.

flow.parent: For a stuck child, ask: are the atoms metals, non-metals, or one of each? One child can play alone or with you.
flow.context: In this step of Give, Share or Pool you play the first twelve material cards.

flow.do: Play the last twelve cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Twelve more cards. This time, also say one thing the material will do. A good answer earns one more point.
flow.kid: Play twelve more cards. Say one thing each material will do.
flow.context: In this step of Give, Share or Pool you play the last twelve cards. You also say what each material will do.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 24 cards into three piles by bond.
flow.say: Sort the cards into three piles: ionic, covalent and metallic. Look at the ionic pile. What do all those materials have in common?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into three piles. What is the same in the ionic pile?

check.q: Calcium is a metal and fluorine is a non-metal. Which bond joins them?
check.why: A metal atom gives electrons to a non-metal atom, and the ions attract each other. If you chose covalent, remember that sharing happens between non-metals. Metallic bonds need metal atoms only.

flow.context: This is the last step of Give, Share or Pool. You sort the material cards into ionic, covalent and metallic piles.

games.title: Give and Take: an ion card game
games.context: This is a card game about ionic compounds. Metal cards give electrons and non-metal cards take them. You lay down a set when the electrons given equal the electrons taken.

setup.art: Thirty-two cards in a pile, some marked GIVES in blue and some marked TAKES in red, with five cards dealt to each of two players.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 32 cards. Shuffle them and deal 5 to each player.

setup.art: A child laying down one card marked 'Calcium GIVES 2' beside two cards marked 'Chlorine TAKES 1'.
setup.caption: 2. Lay down a set where electrons given equal electrons taken.

setup.art: A score sheet with the names calcium chloride and sodium oxide written on it, and a pencil.
setup.caption: 3. Name your compound from the name sheet. Score 1 point for each card.

printables.title: 32 atom cards: 15 metal cards that give electrons and 17 non-metal cards that take electrons
Name sheet and score sheet: how to name a compound, and a row for each player's points
items: To name a compound, say the metal first. Then say the non-metal with its ending changed to -ide.
Chlorine becomes chloride. Fluorine becomes fluoride. Oxygen becomes oxide. Sulphur becomes sulphide.
Sodium with chlorine is sodium chloride, which is table salt.
Calcium with oxygen is calcium oxide, which is quicklime.
Sodium with fluorine is sodium fluoride, which is in toothpaste.
Aluminium with oxygen is aluminium oxide, which is what rubies are mostly made of.
Magnesium with chlorine is magnesium chloride, which is in sea salt.
Player 1 points: ____   Player 2 points: ____   Player 3 points: ____

rules: Shuffle the cards. Deal 5 to each player. Put the rest face down as the pile.
On your turn, take one card from the pile. Then you may lay down one set.
A set has one kind of metal and one kind of non-metal. The electrons given must equal the electrons taken.
One calcium gives 2, so it needs two chlorines, which take 1 each. Two aluminiums give 6, so they need three oxygens.
Say the name of your compound. Score 1 point for each card in the set.
If you cannot lay a set, your turn ends. You keep your cards.
The game ends when the pile is empty and nobody can lay a set. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Lay all 32 cards face up. Try to put every card into a set, with none left over. It can be done.

flow.do: Cut out the 32 cards. Read the name sheet together. Deal 5 cards to each player.
flow.say: A metal card gives electrons. A non-metal card takes them. A compound is finished when every electron given has been taken. Then its plus charges equal its minus charges.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read the name sheet. Take 5 cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Give and Take. You set up the atom cards and read how to name a compound.

flow.do: Play two practice turns with the cards face up. Build sodium chloride first, then calcium chloride.
flow.say: Sodium gives 1 and chlorine takes 1. So one of each makes a set. Calcium gives 2. How many chlorines does one calcium need?
flow.kid: Sodium gives 1. Chlorine takes 1. How many chlorines does calcium need?

ask.q: Why does one calcium need two chlorines?
good: Calcium gives 2 electrons, and each chlorine takes only 1.
The electrons given must equal the electrons taken.

flow.parent: Let your child move the cards. The matching is easier to see than to hear.
flow.context: In this step of Give and Take you practise building sodium chloride and calcium chloride with the cards face up.

flow.do: Play the game. Each player takes a card and lays a set if they can. Write the points on the score sheet.
flow.say: Take a card. Can you lay a set? Count the electrons given and the electrons taken. Say the name of your compound.
flow.kid: Take a card. Lay a set if you can. Name your compound.
flow.parent: A child playing alone lays all the cards face up and tries to use every one. One answer uses sodium oxide, magnesium chloride and aluminium oxide.
flow.context: In this step of Give and Take you play the game and name each compound you make.

flow.do: Count the points. Lay the biggest set on the table and count its charges together.
flow.say: Look at aluminium oxide. Two aluminiums give 3 each. Three oxygens take 2 each. Count both sides. Are they equal?
flow.kid: Count the electrons given. Count the electrons taken. Are they equal?

check.q: Magnesium gives 2 electrons. Chlorine takes 1. How many chlorines join one magnesium?
check.why: One magnesium gives 2 electrons, and each chlorine takes 1, so two chlorines are needed. If you chose one, an electron would be left over. The compound is magnesium chloride.

flow.context: This is the last step of Give and Take. You check that the electrons given equal the electrons taken in your biggest set.

experiments.title: Three Solids, Three Tests: press, water and heat
experiments.question: Salt, candle wax and aluminium foil are all solids. What does each one do when it is pressed, put in water and heated over a candle?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which solid will break when pressed? Which will dissolve in water? Which will melt over a candle within one minute? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use pieces of about the same size, each as big as a pea. The same person presses every piece, as hard as they can, with the same spoon. Use the same amount of water and stir each tumbler 30 times. Hold the spoon at the same height over the same flame. Heat each solid for a slow count of 60. Only the solid changes.

materials.item: crystal salt, also called rock salt or kal uppu. Fine table salt works if you have no crystals.
a plain white candle, to cut three pea-sized pieces of wax from its base
aluminium foil, torn into three pieces as big as your palm and rolled into pea-sized balls
old steel spoons, one for pressing and one for heating
a steel plate and a sheet of paper folded in half
small tumblers, each half full of water
a second candle or a diya in a holder, and a matchbox
a thick folded cloth or kitchen tongs, to hold the hot spoon
a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up lights the candle and holds the spoon over the flame. Tie back long hair. Heat only about ten grains of salt, and keep faces away, because a hot salt grain can crack and jump. The spoon stays hot for some minutes, so put it on the steel plate to cool. Do not taste anything after it has been heated.
experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows: salt, wax and foil. Make three columns: pressed, in water and heated. Write what you saw in each box.
experiments.context: In this experiment you press, wet and heat three solids: salt, candle wax and aluminium foil. Each one behaves in its own way, and that shows how its atoms hold on to each other.

setup.art: A steel plate with a salt crystal, a pea-sized piece of white wax and a small ball of aluminium foil in a row, and a steel spoon beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Put a salt crystal, a piece of wax and a foil ball on a plate.

setup.art: A child's hand pressing the back of a steel spoon down on a folded sheet of paper that covers a salt crystal on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 2. Cover each solid with folded paper. Press it hard with the back of a spoon.

setup.art: Three small tumblers of water in a row, one with salt at the bottom, one with a piece of wax floating and one with a foil ball, and a spoon stirring the first.
setup.caption: 3. Put a fresh piece of each solid in water. Stir 30 times.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand holding a steel spoon with a cloth over a candle flame, with a few grains of salt in the bowl of the spoon, while a child watches from a step back.
setup.caption: 4. A grown-up heats each solid in a spoon for a slow count of 60.

flow.do: Put the salt, the wax pieces and the foil balls on the plate. Ask for the three guesses and the reasons. Write them down.
flow.say: Here are salt, wax and foil. We will press each one, put each one in water, and heat each one. What do you think each will do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the salt, wax and foil. Guess what each will do. Say why.

ask.q: Which one do you think will be the hardest to melt, and why?
good: The foil, because it is metal.
The salt, because it never melts in cooking.
Any guess with a reason.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect the metal to be the only one that will not melt.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Solids, Three Tests. You guess what salt, wax and foil will do before you test them.

flow.do: Draw the table. Put the salt crystal on the plate and cover it with the folded paper. Your child presses hard with the back of a spoon. Lift the paper and look. Do the same with the wax and the foil ball.
flow.say: Press as hard as you can, then lift the paper. What happened to the salt? Now press the wax. Now press the foil. Write what you see each time.
flow.kid: Cover the salt. Press hard with the spoon. Look. Then press the wax and the foil.
flow.parent: The paper stops pieces flying. A salt crystal cracks with a small snap into pieces with flat sides. With fine salt, press a pinch between two spoons and listen for the crunch.

check.q: In Three Solids, Three Tests, why does the same person press every solid?
options: So each solid gets the same push
check.why: A stronger push could break something that a weaker push would not. If you chose another answer, remember that a fair test changes only one thing. Here that one thing is the solid.

flow.context: In this step of Three Solids, Three Tests you press salt, wax and foil with the back of a spoon.

flow.do: Put a quarter teaspoon of salt in the first tumbler. Put a piece of wax in the second and a foil ball in the third. Your child stirs each one 30 times and writes what they see.
flow.say: Stir each tumbler 30 times. Count aloud. Which solid can you still see? Which one has gone into the water?
flow.kid: Put each solid in water. Stir 30 times. Which one can you still see?
flow.parent: The salt dissolves. The wax floats and the foil ball floats or sinks, and neither changes.
flow.context: In this step of Three Solids, Three Tests you stir salt, wax and foil in water.

flow.do: Light the candle. Put about ten grains of salt in the heating spoon. Hold the spoon with the cloth, just above the tip of the flame. Count slowly to 60 together. Then heat a fresh foil ball the same way. Heat the wax last.
flow.say: I will hold the spoon. Stand one step back and count slowly to 60 with me. Watch the solid. Tell me the moment anything changes.
flow.kid: Stand one step back. Count to 60. Watch the solid in the spoon.
flow.parent: Salt and foil stay solid. A grain of salt may crack and jump. Wax melts to a clear liquid within about 15 seconds, so heat it last to keep the spoon clean. Soot on the spoon wipes off when it is cool.
flow.context: In this step of Three Solids, Three Tests a grown-up heats salt, foil and wax over a candle.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Did any two solids behave the same way in all three tests?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Salt and foil both stayed solid over the flame. What test tells them apart?
good: Pressing. The salt cracked and the foil only flattened.
Water. The salt dissolved and the foil did not.

ask.q: What might be different about the way the atoms hold on in each solid?
good: In wax the pieces let go of each other easily.
In salt they hold tightly but cannot slide.
In foil they hold and can still slide.

flow.parent: The reason: the three solids are held in three ways. Salt is plus and minus ions in a fixed pattern. They hold tightly, so salt does not melt. If a layer slips, like charges meet and push apart, so salt cracks. Wax is molecules that hold each other weakly, so it squashes and melts. Foil is metal atoms that share their outer electrons. The atoms can slide and still be held, so foil flattens.
flow.think: Sugar also cracks when pressed and dissolves in water. What test might tell sugar from salt?
flow.context: This is the last step of Three Solids, Three Tests. You say what the three tests show about salt, wax and foil.

experiments.title: Dry Salt, Wet Salt: when does salt carry electricity?
experiments.question: Which of these carry electricity? Test a steel spoon, a candle, dry sugar, dry salt, plain water, wet sugar and wet salt.
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which things will make the tester bubble? Will dry salt and wet salt give the same result? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same tester for every test, and do not move the pencils. Hold the two probes one finger-width apart each time. Count slowly to 20 for every test. Use 2 teaspoons of each powder, and add 1 teaspoon of the same water to each. Wipe both probes dry with a clean cloth after every test. Test the salt last, so that no salt reaches the sugar.
results_table: Bubbles at the pencil tips: many, few or none

materials.item: a 9-volt battery, the small box-shaped kind, with a snap clip that has a red wire and a black wire
ordinary wooden pencils, sharpened at both ends. If a pencil has a rubber on the end, a grown-up cuts that end off.
a clear glass tumbler of tap water, with 1 teaspoon of cooking soda stirred in
a strip of cardboard from a medicine box, longer than the tumbler is wide
aluminium foil, a piece 30 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide, folded twice along its length into a flat ribbon
a clothes clip or sticky tape
a steel spoon and a candle
dry plates or saucers that are not metal: ceramic, glass or plastic
sugar and fine table salt
drinking water in a small cup, a teaspoon, and a clean dry cloth
a torch or a phone light, to see the bubbles

experiments.safety: Use only a 9-volt battery. Never use a wall socket or a charger. Do not let the bare ends of the red and black wires touch each other, because the battery gets hot. Do the wet salt test only once, for a count of 20, in a room with a window open. Do not taste the powders after the test. Wash the saucers afterwards.
experiments.record: Draw a table with seven rows: steel spoon, candle, dry sugar, dry salt, plain water, wet sugar and wet salt. Beside each, write many, few or none.
experiments.context: In this experiment you build a bubble tester from a 9-volt battery and two pencils. You use it to find out which things carry electricity, and whether salt carries it dry or wet.

setup.art: Two pencils sharpened at both ends pushed through a cardboard strip that lies across a glass tumbler of water, with their lower tips under the water about two centimetres apart.
setup.caption: 1. Stand two pencils in soda water, 2 centimetres apart.

setup.art: A 9-volt battery with its red wire twisted round the top tip of one pencil, a foil ribbon clipped to the top tip of the other pencil, and the black wire and the foil ribbon ending as two loose ends.
setup.caption: 2. Red wire to one pencil. Foil ribbon to the other. The two loose ends are your probes.

setup.art: A child's hands touching the two loose ends to a steel spoon, and fine bubbles rising from both pencil tips in the tumbler.
setup.caption: 3. Touch both probes to a thing. Bubbles in the tumbler mean it carries electricity.

setup.art: Two white ceramic saucers, one with a dry heap of salt and one with a wet heap of salt, each with the two probes pushed into it a finger-width apart.
setup.caption: 4. Test dry salt on a saucer that is not metal. Then add a teaspoon of water and test again.

flow.do: Show your child the spoon, the candle, the sugar, the salt and the water. Ask which will carry electricity, and why. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: We will test seven things. Which do you think will carry electricity? Will dry salt and wet salt be the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which things carry electricity. Will dry and wet salt differ? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think wet salt will or will not carry electricity?
good: Water carries electricity.
Salt is not a metal, so it will not.
Any guess with a reason.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say that the water does the carrying.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dry Salt, Wet Salt. You guess which things will carry electricity before you test them.

flow.do: Push the two pencils through the cardboard, 2 centimetres apart. Rest the cardboard on the tumbler of soda water, with the lower tips under water. Twist the bare end of the red wire round the top tip of one pencil. Wrap one end of the foil ribbon tightly round the top tip of the other pencil. Hold it with the clip. Now touch the free end of the foil to the bare end of the black wire.
flow.say: The black wire and the loose end of the foil are our two probes. Touch them together and watch the pencil tips in the water. What do you see? Now pull them apart.
flow.kid: Touch the two probes together. Watch the pencil tips. Then pull the probes apart.
flow.parent: Fine bubbles should stream from both lower tips within a few seconds, and stop when the probes part. If not, press the wire and the foil harder against the pencil tips. The soda water is only part of the tester. It stays the same all through.

check.q: In the bubble tester, what do bubbles at the pencil tips tell you?
options: Electricity is passing between the probes
check.why: Electricity must go all the way round, through the thing between the probes and through the water. Bubbles form only when it does. If you chose heat, feel the tumbler: it stays cool.

flow.context: In this step of Dry Salt, Wet Salt you build the bubble tester and check that it works.

flow.do: Your child holds both probes on the steel spoon, one finger-width apart, for a slow count of 20. Write many, few or none. Do the same on the side of the candle.
flow.say: Hold both probes on the spoon. Do not let them touch each other. Count to 20 and watch the pencil tips. Now try the candle.
flow.kid: Hold both probes on the spoon. Count to 20. Then test the candle.
flow.parent: The spoon gives many bubbles. The candle gives none.
flow.context: In this step of Dry Salt, Wet Salt you test a steel spoon and a candle with the bubble tester.

flow.do: Make a heap of 2 teaspoons of sugar on one dry saucer and 2 teaspoons of salt on another. Push both probes into the sugar, one finger-width apart, and count to 20. Wipe the probes. Test the dry salt. Wipe the probes. Then pour 1 teaspoon of water on the third saucer and test the small pool.
flow.say: Push the probes into the dry sugar. Count to 20. Now wipe them and try the dry salt. Then try the small pool of plain water. Write each result.
flow.kid: Test the dry sugar. Wipe the probes. Test the dry salt. Then test plain water.
flow.parent: The saucers must not be metal, because a metal plate would carry the electricity itself. Dry sugar and dry salt give none. Plain water gives none, or a very few slow bubbles, because tap water has a little salt in it. On a damp monsoon day, salt takes in water from the air and may give a few bubbles. Warm it in a dry pan for a minute first.
flow.context: In this step of Dry Salt, Wet Salt you test dry sugar, dry salt and plain water.

flow.do: Add 1 teaspoon of water to the sugar heap and stir with a matchstick. Test it for a count of 20. Wipe the probes. Add 1 teaspoon of water to the salt heap and stir with a fresh matchstick. Test it for a count of 20.
flow.say: Now we wet the sugar and test it. Then we wet the salt and test it. Watch the pencil tips closely each time. Which one changed?
flow.kid: Wet the sugar and test it. Wipe the probes. Wet the salt and test it.
flow.parent: Wet sugar gives the same as plain water. Wet salt gives many bubbles at once, and it may fizz at the probes too. The salt paste may turn grey or green where the probes react with it. Throw the paste away and wash the saucer.
flow.context: In this step of Dry Salt, Wet Salt you wet the sugar and the salt, and test each again.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. What did the water change about the salt?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Plain water gave almost no bubbles, and wet sugar gave almost none. So what carried the electricity in the wet salt?
good: Something from the salt.
The salt, once it was in the water.
Charged particles from the salt.

ask.q: The spoon carried electricity dry. Why might a metal need no water?
good: Something in the metal can already move.
Its electrons are free.

flow.parent: The reason: electricity passes only where charged particles can move. Salt is made of charged particles called ions. In dry salt each ion is held in place by its neighbours, so nothing can move. Water pulls the ions apart, and they drift through the water and carry the electricity. Sugar is made of molecules with no charge, so wet sugar carries almost none. In the steel spoon, electrons are free to move all the time.
flow.think: A doorbell button near the sea has a crust of dry salt on it. What might happen on a misty morning?
flow.context: This is the last step of Dry Salt, Wet Salt. You say what your results show about dry salt and wet salt.

activities.title: Bend or Break: a paper clip and a salt crystal

materials.item: a steel paper clip, or a safety pin with its point closed
aluminium foil, a piece as big as your palm
big crystals of salt, also called rock salt or kal uppu. If you have none, use a pinch of fine salt.
a steel spoon, a steel plate and a sheet of paper folded in half

schedule.what: Bend a paper clip, flatten a ball of foil and press a salt crystal. Notice which ones change shape and which one breaks.

activities.safety: Cover the salt with the folded paper before pressing, so that no piece flies towards the eyes.
activities.record: Write one sentence that begins 'I wonder why'.
activities.context: This is a quick activity to start the unit. You press and bend three hard things, and notice that metal changes shape but salt breaks.

setup.art: A child's hands opening a steel paper clip into a straight wire.
setup.caption: 1. Bend a paper clip open. Bend it back. Does it break?

setup.art: A small ball of aluminium foil on a steel plate beside a flat shiny disc of foil, with the back of a spoon above them.
setup.caption: 2. Roll foil into a ball. Press it flat with a spoon.

setup.art: A salt crystal on a steel plate, half covered by a folded sheet of paper, with the back of a spoon pressing down on the paper.
setup.caption: 3. Cover a salt crystal with paper. Press hard. Look at the pieces.

flow.do: Put the paper clip, the foil and the salt crystals on the plate. Ask the question below and write down the guess.
flow.say: All three of these are hard solids. If you press or bend each one as hard as you can, what will happen? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the clip, foil and salt. What will pressing do? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Bend or Break. You guess what will happen when you bend a paper clip and press a salt crystal.

flow.do: Your child bends the paper clip open and back once. Then they roll the foil into a ball and press it flat with the back of the spoon.
flow.say: Bend the clip open, and bend it back. Is it still in one piece? Now roll the foil into a ball and press it flat.
flow.kid: Bend the clip open and back. Roll the foil. Press it flat.
flow.parent: Bend the clip only once or twice. Many bends in the same place will break it in the end.
flow.context: In this step of Bend or Break you bend a steel paper clip and flatten a ball of aluminium foil.

flow.do: Put one salt crystal on the plate. Cover it with the folded paper. Your child presses hard with the back of the spoon until they hear a crack. Lift the paper and look at the pieces.
flow.say: Now the salt. Press hard on the paper until you hear something. Lift the paper. What happened? Look closely at the pieces.
flow.kid: Cover the salt. Press hard until it cracks. Look at the pieces.

ask.q: What do you notice about the pieces of salt?
good: They are smaller crystals.
Some have flat sides and sharp corners.
It did not squash. It broke.

flow.parent: With fine salt, press a pinch between two spoons. You will hear and feel the grains crunch.
flow.context: In this step of Bend or Break you press a salt crystal under paper with the back of a spoon.

flow.do: Ask your child what they noticed and what they wonder. Write down one 'I wonder why' sentence. Do not explain yet.
flow.say: The clip and the foil changed shape and stayed whole. The salt broke. What do you wonder about that?
flow.kid: What did you notice? Say one thing you wonder about.
flow.parent: Keep the sentence. The experiment Three Solids, Three Tests and the model Slide a Row will answer it.

check.q: A steel paper clip is bent once. A salt crystal is pressed hard. What happens?
options: The clip bends and the salt cracks
check.why: A metal changes shape and stays in one piece. A salt crystal does not bend, and it splits into pieces. If you chose another answer, try both again and watch closely.

flow.context: This is the last step of Bend or Break. You say what you noticed about the metal and the salt, and what you wonder.

activities.title: Slide a Row: a salt model and a metal model

materials.item: coins of the same kind, for example one-rupee coins. Carrom coins also work, 8 black and 8 white.
a ruler
a tray, or a large book laid flat
rice grains

schedule.what: Build a model of salt and a model of a metal from coins. Slide a row in each, and see which one comes apart.

activities.record: Draw the salt model before and after the slide. Circle the places where like charges face each other.
activities.context: In this activity you build a flat model of a salt crystal and a metal from 16 coins. Sliding one row shows why salt cracks and metal bends.

setup.art: Sixteen coins on a tray in four rows of four, placed heads up and tails up in turns like the squares of a chessboard.
setup.caption: 1. Lay 16 coins in 4 rows of 4. Heads and tails take turns, like a chessboard.

setup.art: The same sixteen coins with a ruler pushing the top two rows one place to the right, so that along the middle line heads face heads and tails face tails.
setup.caption: 2. Slide the top two rows one place. Look at the middle line.

setup.art: Sixteen coins all heads up in four rows of four, with rice grains scattered in the gaps between them, and a ruler pushing the top two rows sideways.
setup.caption: 3. Turn all coins heads up. Scatter rice between them. Slide again.

flow.do: Lay the 16 coins on the tray in 4 rows of 4, touching. Heads up means a plus sodium ion. Tails up means a minus chloride ion. Place them in turns, so that every coin has the other kind on each side.
flow.say: Heads is a plus ion and tails is a minus ion. Plus and minus attract. Lay them so that every coin touches only the other kind along its sides.
flow.kid: Lay 16 coins in a square. Heads and tails take turns.
flow.parent: With carrom coins, use white for plus and black for minus.
flow.context: This is the first step of Slide a Row. You build a flat model of a salt crystal from 16 coins.

flow.do: Ask your child to count the heads and the tails. Then point to one coin in the middle and ask how many of the other kind touch its sides. Ask which one is its partner.
flow.say: How many plus ions are there, and how many minus? Look at this plus ion in the middle. How many minus ions touch its sides? Which one is its partner?
flow.kid: Count heads and tails. Pick a middle coin. How many opposite neighbours?

ask.q: Which minus ion belongs to this plus ion?
good: None of them more than the others.
All four hold it equally.
There are no pairs.

flow.parent: There are 8 of each. A middle coin has 4 opposite neighbours. In a real crystal there are layers above and below too, so each ion has 6.
flow.context: In this step of Slide a Row you count the ions and the neighbours in the coin model of salt.

flow.do: Lay the ruler along the top two rows. Push them one coin to the right, keeping the rows straight. Look at the line where the top half meets the bottom half.
flow.say: I will slide the top two rows one place. Look at the middle line now. What is facing what? What do like charges do to each other?
flow.kid: Slide the top two rows one place. What faces what now?

ask.q: What will happen along the middle line in a real crystal?
good: Plus faces plus and minus faces minus, so they repel.
The two halves push apart.
The crystal cracks there.

flow.parent: This is why salt cracked in Bend or Break. A push slides one layer, like charges meet, and the layers push apart along a flat face.
flow.context: In this step of Slide a Row you slide the top half of the salt model one place sideways.

flow.do: Now turn all 16 coins heads up, back in a 4 by 4 square. Each coin is a metal atom that has given its outer electron to the pool. Scatter the rice grains in the gaps as the free electrons. Slide the top two rows one place again.
flow.say: Now every coin is a plus metal atom. The rice grains are the free electrons between them. Slide the top two rows again. Has anything changed along the middle line?
flow.kid: Turn all coins heads up. Scatter rice between them. Slide a row again.
flow.parent: After the slide the metal model looks just as it did before. Every atom still has electrons between it and its neighbours. So a metal changes shape and stays whole.

check.q: Why does a salt crystal crack when one layer of ions slips sideways?
check.why: After the slip, plus ions face plus ions and minus face minus. Like charges repel, so the layers push apart. If you chose another answer, slide the coin model again and look at the middle line.

flow.context: This is the last step of Slide a Row. You build a metal model with coins and rice, and slide a row in it.

activities.title: Give, Share, Pool: move the electrons yourself

materials.item: paper circles as big as a saucer, cut from old newspaper
chana or rajma, as outer electrons
a pencil or a marker

schedule.what: Use paper atoms and chana electrons to act out an ionic, a covalent and a metallic bond. Then draw all three.

activities.record: Draw three pictures: salt, water and copper. Show where the outer electrons are in each.
activities.context: In this activity paper circles are atoms and chana are their outer electrons. You move the chana to show the three kinds of bond: giving, sharing and pooling.

setup.art: Two paper circles labelled Na and Cl on a table, with one chana on the Na circle and seven on the Cl circle, and a child's hand moving the single chana across.
setup.caption: 1. Sodium has 1 outer electron. Chlorine has 7. Move sodium's electron to chlorine.

setup.art: A paper circle labelled O overlapping two smaller circles labelled H, with two chana lying in each overlap.
setup.caption: 2. Oxygen and hydrogen share. Put two electrons in each overlap.

setup.art: Four paper circles labelled Cu in a square with four chana loose in the space between them.
setup.caption: 3. Four copper atoms pool their electrons in the middle.

flow.do: Label the nine circles: Na, Cl, O, H, H and four marked Cu. Count out the chana. Na gets 1, Cl gets 7 and O gets 6. Each H and each Cu gets 1.
flow.say: Each circle is an atom. Each chana is one of its outer electrons. Sodium has 1, chlorine has 7, oxygen has 6, and hydrogen and copper have 1 each.
flow.kid: Label the circles. Put the chana on each atom.
flow.context: This is the first step of Give, Share, Pool. You make paper atoms and give each one its outer electrons.

flow.do: Put Na and Cl side by side. Ask your child to move sodium's one chana onto chlorine. Write a plus sign on Na and a minus sign on Cl.
flow.say: Sodium holds its outer electron weakly, and chlorine attracts it strongly. Move it across. Sodium has lost a minus charge. What charge does sodium have now? What about chlorine?
flow.kid: Move sodium's electron to chlorine. Which atom is plus now? Which is minus?

ask.q: Why do the two ions now hold on to each other?
good: One is plus and one is minus.
Opposite charges attract.

flow.parent: Chlorine now has 8 outer electrons. For many atoms, a set of 8 is a steady arrangement. This is an ionic bond.
flow.context: In this step of Give, Share, Pool you move one electron from sodium to chlorine to make two ions.

flow.do: Lay O so that it overlaps each H a little. In each overlap, put one chana from the hydrogen and one from the oxygen. Count the chana that oxygen can reach, and the chana that each hydrogen can reach.
flow.say: Oxygen and hydrogen are both non-metals, so neither gives an electron away. They share. Put one electron from each atom in the overlap. How many electrons can oxygen count now?
flow.kid: Overlap the circles. Put two electrons in each overlap. Count oxygen's electrons.
flow.parent: Oxygen counts 8, and each hydrogen counts 2, which is a full set for hydrogen. Each shared pair is one covalent bond.
flow.context: In this step of Give, Share, Pool you make a water molecule by sharing electrons between oxygen and hydrogen.

flow.do: Lay the four Cu circles in a square. Move each one's chana into the space in the middle. Push the chana along with a finger. Then ask your child to draw all three models.
flow.say: Each copper atom puts its outer electron into a shared pool. Push the pool along. That flow is an electric current. Now draw salt, water and copper, and show where the electrons are.
flow.kid: Pool the copper electrons in the middle. Push them along. Draw all three bonds.

check.q: In which bond do the outer electrons belong to all the atoms together?
check.why: In a metal the outer electrons leave their own atoms and move among all of them. In an ionic bond an electron moves to one other atom. In a covalent bond two atoms share a pair.

flow.context: This is the last step of Give, Share, Pool. You pool the electrons of four copper atoms and draw the three kinds of bond.

activities.title: Ion Hunt on Labels: find the ionic compounds at home

materials.item: packets and tubes that list their ingredients. Good ones are a salt packet, toothpaste, an ORS sachet, bottled drinking water and cooking soda.
a notebook page and a pencil

schedule.what: Read the ingredient lists on five packets and find the names of ionic compounds.

activities.record: Make three columns: the packet, the ionic compound, and the metal in it. Write at least five rows.
activities.context: In this activity you read the labels of things at home and find ionic compounds. Their names usually begin with a metal and end in -ide or -ate.

setup.art: A salt packet, a toothpaste tube, an ORS sachet and a bottle of drinking water lined up on a table with their ingredient lists facing forward.
setup.caption: 1. Collect five packets that list their ingredients.

setup.art: A child's finger under the words 'sodium fluoride' on the back of a toothpaste tube.
setup.caption: 2. Look for a metal name followed by a word ending in -ide or -ate.

setup.art: A notebook page with three columns and rows that read: toothpaste, sodium fluoride, sodium.
setup.caption: 3. Write the packet, the compound and the metal.

flow.do: Collect the packets. Read out the clue below and write the metal names on the page.
flow.say: An ionic compound has two words in its name. The first is a metal: sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium or zinc. The second usually ends in -ide or -ate.
flow.kid: Listen to the clue. Write the five metal names.
flow.parent: Chloride, fluoride and oxide end in -ide. Carbonate, sulphate, citrate and iodate end in -ate.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ion Hunt on Labels. You learn the clue for spotting an ionic compound in a list of ingredients.

flow.do: Your child reads each ingredient list and writes down every ionic compound they find. Help with long words.
flow.say: Read the list on each packet. Each time you find a metal name with a second word, write it down. Which packet has the most?
flow.kid: Read each label. Write every name that starts with a metal.

ask.q: Which metal turned up most often?
good: Sodium.
Sodium and potassium.

flow.parent: Likely finds in salt are sodium chloride and potassium iodate. Toothpaste has sodium fluoride or calcium carbonate. ORS has potassium chloride and sodium citrate. Bottled water often lists magnesium sulphate.
flow.context: In this step of Ion Hunt on Labels you read five ingredient lists and write down the ionic compounds.

flow.do: Look at the ORS sachet together. Find the one ingredient that is not ionic. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: ORS has salts and one more thing, glucose. Glucose is carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Is it ionic or covalent? Why does the label call the salts electrolytes?
flow.kid: Find glucose on the ORS packet. Is it ionic or covalent?

check.q: Which of these names is an ionic compound?
check.why: Potassium is a metal and chlorine is a non-metal, so potassium chloride is made of ions. Glucose and carbon dioxide have only non-metal atoms, so they are covalent molecules.

flow.context: This is the last step of Ion Hunt on Labels. You find the one covalent ingredient in ORS and say why the salts are called electrolytes.

projects.title: Powder Detective: which kitchen things split into ions in water?

materials.item: the bubble tester from Dry Salt, Wet Salt: a 9-volt battery, two pencils in soda water, and two probes
small glass or plastic cups. Do not use steel katoris, because steel carries electricity.
fine salt, cooking soda and sugar
glucose powder, or a second kind of sugar such as kalkandu or mishri, crushed
lemon juice and vinegar. If you have no vinegar, use the water from soaked tamarind.
drinking water, a tablespoon, a teaspoon and a clean dry cloth
a notebook page and a pencil

projects.safety: Use only a 9-volt battery. Test each cup for a count of 20 and no longer. Keep a window open. Do not drink the liquids after testing. Pour them down the sink.

schedule.what: Find out which atoms are in each of six kitchen things, and predict which will carry electricity in water.
Dissolve each one, test it with the bubble tester, and compare the results with your predictions.

projects.record: Make a table with four columns: the thing, its atoms, my prediction, and the bubbles I saw. Write one row for plain water and one for each of the six things.
projects.context: In this two-day project you predict which kitchen powders and liquids are made of ions, and then test them. You use the bubble tester from the experiment Dry Salt, Wet Salt. In that experiment, wet salt made the tester bubble and wet sugar did not.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows for salt, cooking soda, sugar, glucose, lemon juice and vinegar, and a column of predictions written as yes or no.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: write the atoms in each thing. Predict yes or no.

setup.art: Seven small glass cups in a row, each with a paper label and a little clear liquid.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: dissolve each thing in 3 tablespoons of water. Use glass or plastic cups.

setup.art: A child holding two probes in one glass cup, a finger-width apart, with the pencil tester bubbling in a tumbler beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Dip both probes in each cup for a count of 20. Wipe them after each test.

flow.do: Day 1. Draw the table. Read out the atoms in each thing from the note below. Your child writes them, then predicts yes or no for each: will it carry electricity in water?
flow.say: Use the guide. A metal with a non-metal is ionic, and ions carry electricity in water. Non-metals alone make molecules. Write yes or no for each thing, and say why.
flow.kid: Write the atoms in each thing. Predict yes or no. Say why.
flow.parent: Salt is sodium and chlorine. Cooking soda is sodium with hydrogen, carbon and oxygen. Sugar, glucose, lemon juice and vinegar are all carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
flow.context: This is the first step of Powder Detective. You predict which kitchen things will carry electricity in water.

flow.do: Day 2. Label the seven cups. Put 3 tablespoons of drinking water in each. Leave the first as plain water. Stir half a teaspoon of each powder, or 1 teaspoon of each liquid, into the others. Set up the bubble tester.
flow.say: Every cup gets the same amount of the same water. Then only one thing differs from cup to cup. Stir until each powder has dissolved.
flow.kid: Put the same water in every cup. Stir one thing into each.
flow.context: In this step of Powder Detective you dissolve six kitchen things in equal amounts of water.

flow.do: Dip both probes into the plain water, one finger-width apart, for a count of 20. Write many, few or none. Wipe the probes dry. Test the sugar, the glucose, the vinegar, the lemon juice, the cooking soda and the salt, in that order.
flow.say: Dip both probes in, and do not let them touch. Count to 20 and watch the pencil tips. Wipe the probes before the next cup.
flow.kid: Dip both probes in. Count to 20. Wipe the probes. Test the next cup.
flow.parent: Sugar and glucose give the same as plain water. Cooking soda and salt give many bubbles. Lemon juice gives bubbles, and vinegar usually gives a few.
flow.context: In this step of Powder Detective you test seven cups with the bubble tester and write down the bubbles.

flow.do: Compare the results with the predictions. Ask your child to say what they predicted, what they found, and why they think it happened. Then read the note below.
flow.say: Which predictions were right? Which were wrong? Lemon juice and vinegar have no metal atoms. What might be happening to their molecules in water?
flow.kid: Which guesses were right? Which thing surprised you? Why might that be?

ask.q: The guide said lemon juice has only non-metals. The tester still bubbled. What does that tell you about the guide?
good: The guide is a good start, but it is not always right.
A test can show what a rule misses.
Some molecules must make ions in water.

flow.parent: The reason: lemon juice and vinegar hold acids. An acid is a covalent molecule, but in water some of its molecules split into ions. Lemon juice also holds a little potassium salt from the fruit. So a rule from the kinds of atoms is a first guess, and the test decides.
flow.context: This is the last step of Powder Detective. You compare the bubble results with your predictions.

challenges.title: Tank-Full Alarm: make the tester bubble when the water reaches the line
challenges.problem: Water tanks on roofs overflow when nobody is watching, and good water is wasted. Many homes have an alarm that sounds when the tank is full. Build a small one. Your tank is a glass or plastic tumbler. Your alarm is the bubble tester from Dry Salt, Wet Salt. It bubbles when electricity passes between its two probes. The tester must start to bubble when the water reaches a line 2 centimetres below the rim.
constraints: The tester must not bubble while the water is below the line.
It must bubble within a count of 5 after the water reaches the line.
It must stop when you pour some water out again.
The two probes must never touch each other.
Use tank water made of 1 tumbler of water with a quarter teaspoon of salt. You may use only tape, cardboard, foil and things from the kitchen.
materials: the bubble tester from Dry Salt, Wet Salt: a 9-volt battery, two pencils in soda water, and two probes
a glass or plastic tumbler, or a clear plastic bottle cut in half, as the tank. A steel tumbler will not do.
a jug of water with a quarter teaspoon of salt stirred in
sticky tape, cardboard and extra aluminium foil
a marker, to draw the line 2 centimetres below the rim
a bottle cap or a piece of cork, if you want to try a float
general: Tape both probes inside the tank with their ends at the line, a finger-width apart.
Tape one probe at the bottom of the tank and the other with its end at the line.
Hang both probes from a cardboard strip laid across the rim, so that their ends reach down to the line.
creative: Float a bottle cap wrapped in foil on the water. Fix both probes above it at the line. The rising cap touches both and joins them, so this works even with pure water.
Add a second pair of probes halfway up. Then the tester can tell you 'half full' as well as 'full'.
Use a plastic bottle as the tank and push the probes in through two small holes at the line. Seal the holes with wax.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own alarm. It must pass all four tests. It stays quiet below the line, and it bubbles at the line. It stops after you pour water out. Its probes never touch. Draw your design. Write which part of the circuit the tank water completes, and what in the water carries the electricity.
challenges.context: In this challenge you build an alarm that tells when a tank is full. It uses what you found in the experiment Dry Salt, Wet Salt. Water with dissolved salt carries electricity, because its ions can move.

setup.art: A glass tumbler with a line drawn two centimetres below the rim, beside the pencil-and-battery bubble tester and a jug of water.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a line 2 centimetres below the rim of the tank.

setup.art: Two probes taped inside the tumbler with their bare ends at the line, a finger-width apart, and water being poured in slowly from a jug.
setup.caption: 2. Fix the probes. Pour the tank water in slowly.

setup.art: The water touching both probes at the line, and bubbles rising from the pencil tips in the tester.
setup.caption: 3. Do the bubbles start at the line? Pour some out. Do they stop?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Let your child hold both probes in the empty tank and then pour water in without a plan.
flow.say: First, just hold the probes in the tank and pour. When do the bubbles start? Is that at the line? What must you change?
flow.kid: Hold the probes in the tank. Pour water in. When do bubbles start?

ask.q: What decides the moment the bubbles start?
good: The water must touch both probes.
The height of the higher probe.
The water joins the two probes.

ask.q: Why will a steel tumbler not do as the tank?
good: Steel carries electricity, so it would join the probes with no water.
The alarm would bubble all the time.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Tank-Full Alarm. You find out what happens when the probes are held in the tank without a plan.

flow.do: Your child chooses one of the usual solutions and builds it. Pour the tank water in slowly and watch the pencil tips.
flow.say: Choose one way to fix the probes. Build it. I will pour slowly. Say 'now' when the bubbles start. Was the water at the line?
flow.kid: Fix the probes your way. Watch the pencil tips. Say when bubbles start.
flow.parent: The bubbles are slower than with wet salt, because this water is only slightly salty. Use the torch to see them.
flow.context: In this step of the Tank-Full Alarm you build one design and test whether the bubbles start at the line.

flow.do: Test the design against all four rules. Pour water out and in again three times. Then let your child try one creative solution or their own idea.
flow.say: Does it stay quiet below the line? Does it start at the line? Does it stop when I pour water out? Now make it better.
flow.kid: Check all four rules. Then try a new idea of your own.
flow.context: In this step of the Tank-Full Alarm you check your design against the four rules and improve it.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the final design and explain it. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Draw your alarm. Show the path the electricity takes. Which part of the path is the tank water? What in the water carries the electricity?
flow.kid: Draw your alarm. Show the path of the electricity.

check.q: What carries the electricity through slightly salty tank water?
options: Free electrons, as in a wire
check.why: Dissolved salts are split into ions, and the moving ions carry the electricity. Free electrons carry it in a metal. Pure water has very few ions, so it carries very little.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Tank-Full Alarm. You draw your design and explain how the tank water completes the circuit.

items.p: What is an ion?
opts: An atom with an electric charge
items.why: An ion is an atom that has lost or gained electrons, so its plus and minus charges no longer balance.

items.p: Which bond forms when a metal atom gives electrons to a non-metal atom?
items.why: Giving an electron makes a plus ion and a minus ion. Their attraction is an ionic bond.

items.p: A bond made when two atoms share a pair of electrons is called a ____ bond.
items.why: Both atoms attract the shared pair, and that holds them together. Non-metal atoms bond in this way.

items.p: A grain of salt is made of salt molecules.
items.why: False. Salt is a lattice of ions. Each ion has six neighbours of the other kind, and no partner of its own.

items.p: Match each bond to what the outer electrons do.
pairs: Move from one atom to another
Are shared by all the atoms
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The three bonds differ in where the outer electrons end up: given, shared by two, or shared by all.

items.p: Sort these materials by the kind of bond that holds them.
items.a: see items
items.why: A metal with a non-metal is ionic. Non-metals alone are covalent. Metals alone are metallic.

items.p: Why does a metal bend without breaking?
opts: Its atoms slide and still hold
items.why: The free electrons hold the atoms wherever they slide to. If you chose soft atoms, remember that the atoms do not change. Only their places change.

items.p: Dry salt carries electricity.
items.why: False. The ions in dry salt are held in place. Charges must be free to move before they can carry electricity.

items.p: Candle wax melts in seconds over a flame. Why?
opts: Its molecules hold each other weakly
items.why: Melting only lets whole molecules slide past each other. The covalent bonds inside each wax molecule stay unbroken.

items.p: A material that can be beaten into a new shape without breaking is ____.
items.why: Metals are malleable because their atoms can slide to new places and still be held by the free electrons.

items.p: Put these solids in order of melting point, lowest first.
items.why: Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius and wax at about 60. Aluminium melts at 660 and salt at about 800. The two solids made of molecules melt most easily.

items.p: What carries electricity through a copper wire?
items.why: In a metal the outer electrons are free to flow. Ions carry electricity in salt water, and copper has no molecules.

items.p: In Three Solids, Three Tests, salt cracked and foil flattened. Explain why in two sentences.
items.a: In salt, a slipped layer brings like charges together, and they push the crystal apart. In foil, the atoms slide and the free electrons still hold them.
items.why: A strong answer says what happens when a layer slips in each solid. It names like charges for salt and free electrons for metal.

items.p: In Dry Salt, Wet Salt, dry salt gave no bubbles and wet salt gave many. What did the water do?
items.a: The water pulled the ions out of the lattice. Then the ions could move through the water and carry the electricity.
items.why: A strong answer says the ions were already in the dry salt. The water freed them. It did not carry the electricity itself.

items.p: Draw a flat piece of a salt crystal as a pattern of plus and minus ions. Show eight of each.
items.a: Four rows of four circles. Plus and minus take turns along every row and down every column. So each ion has only the other kind beside it.
items.why: A strong drawing has no pairs set apart from the rest. Every plus touches only minuses along its sides.
items.art: A blank square frame with one circle marked plus drawn in the top left corner.

worksheets.title: Why each solid behaves as it does

items.p: Sodium atoms react fiercely. Sodium ions in salt do not. Why?
opts: The ion has already given its electron
items.why: A sodium atom reacts by giving away its outer electron. The ion has no such electron left to give, so it does not react in that way.

items.p: In a salt crystal, how many chloride ions surround each sodium ion?
items.why: Each sodium ion has four chloride ions around it in its own layer, one above and one below. If you chose one, remember that salt has no pairs.

items.p: Melting ice breaks the covalent bonds inside water molecules.
items.why: False. Melting only lets whole water molecules slide past each other. Each molecule is still one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms.

items.p: Why does sugar water carry almost no electricity?
items.why: Sugar dissolves as whole molecules. With no charged particles to drift, almost nothing carries the electricity.

items.p: A substance that carries electricity when dissolved, because its ions move, is an ____.
items.why: Salt and cooking soda are electrolytes. ORS replaces the electrolytes a sick child loses.

items.p: Match each test result to what it tells you.
pairs: Like charges meet when a layer slips
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each result comes from how the particles are held. That is how tests can show a kind of bond that nobody can see.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one carry electricity well?
items.a: see items
items.why: Metals have free electrons, and salt water has free ions. Dry salt, wax and sugar water have no charged particles that can move.

items.p: The formula NaCl means one sodium ion for every chloride ion.
items.why: True. NaCl gives the ratio of the ions in the lattice. It does not stand for a molecule.

items.p: Put these in order to show how wet salt comes to carry electricity.
items: Water molecules pull ions out of the lattice
The ions drift through the water
Plus ions reach the minus wire
a: Water molecules pull ions out of the lattice
The ions drift through the water
Plus ions reach the minus wire
items.why: The ions must be freed before they can move. Once free, plus ions drift one way and minus ions the other.

items.p: Calcium gives 2 electrons and chlorine takes 1. Which formula is right?
items.why: One calcium needs two chlorines to take its 2 electrons. The small 2 after Cl means two chloride ions for each calcium ion.

items.p: Sugar and salt both crack and both dissolve. Describe a test that tells them apart, and say why it works.
items.a: Dissolve each in water and test with the bubble tester. Salt water carries electricity because salt splits into ions. Sugar water carries almost none because sugar stays as molecules with no charge.
items.why: A strong answer names a test where the two differ, and gives the reason in terms of ions and molecules. Heating also works: sugar melts and browns, and salt does not.

items.p: Diamond is covalent, yet it is very hard and does not melt easily. Explain why.
items.a: In diamond every carbon atom is bonded to four others, all through the stone. There are no separate molecules to slide apart. Covalent bonds themselves must break.
items.why: A strong answer separates the strong bonds inside a molecule from the weak attraction between molecules. Diamond has only the strong kind.

items.p: Why must the saucers in Dry Salt, Wet Salt not be made of metal?
items.a: A metal saucer carries electricity itself. The tester would bubble whenever both probes touched it, even with dry salt on top.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the test must show the powder only. Anything else that carries electricity between the probes spoils it.

items.p: Is salt a conductor of electricity?

views.says: No. I tested dry salt, and the tester did not bubble. Salt is an insulator.
Yes. I wetted the same salt, and the tester bubbled at once. Salt is a conductor.
Near the sea, salt is hardly ever fully dry. I treat every salty surface as a conductor, to be safe.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about bonds. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that the ions are in the salt all the time. Another is that they carry electricity only when they are free to move.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer says what stays the same in the salt and what the water changes.

items.p: Draw a piece of metal before and after it is bent. Show the atoms and the free electrons.
items.a: Both drawings show rows of plus atoms with small electron dots in every gap. In the second, some rows have slid sideways, and the dots still fill the gaps.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the electrons between the atoms after the bend. That is why the metal stays in one piece.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, labelled 'before' and 'after'.

items.p: A white powder cracks when pressed and will not melt on a flame. Its solution carries electricity. Which bond?
items.why: Brittle, hard to melt and an electrolyte in water are the three signs of an ionic solid.

items.p: Pencil lead is covalent, yet it carries electricity. What does that show?
items.why: In graphite, each carbon atom has one electron that is free to move. The three types are a guide, and real materials can lie between them.

items.p: Salt lowers the freezing point of water about twice as much as sugar does. Why?
opts: Each unit of salt gives two particles
items.why: Dissolved salt splits into a sodium ion and a chloride ion. Sugar stays as one molecule. This is how Arrhenius showed that ions exist in salt water.

items.p: The kind of bond between atoms can change under very high pressure.
items.why: True. Hydrogen is a gas of molecules on Earth. Squeezed hard enough, it carries electricity like a metal.

items.p: Pure water carries electricity well.
items.why: False. Pure water has very few ions. The salts dissolved in tap water and sweat carry the electricity, which is why wet hands are still dangerous.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they showed.
pairs: A ring of six carbon atoms is flat
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each finding answered a different question about bonds. Where do the ions sit? When do they move? What shape are molecules? Are the three types separate?

items.p: A metal mixed with one or more other elements is called an ____.
items.why: Steel, brass and bell metal are alloys. Atoms of a different size make the layers harder to slide.

items.p: Sort these by what carries the electricity.
items.a: see items
items.why: Metals carry electricity by electrons. Liquids with dissolved salts, including the liquids in your body, carry it by ions.

items.p: Aluminium gives 3 electrons and oxygen takes 2. How many of each make a compound?
items.why: Two aluminiums give 6 electrons, and three oxygens take 6. If you chose 3 and 2, count again: that gives 9 and takes 4.

items.p: Many people think water itself carries electricity. What would you test to find out what really carries it?
items.a: Test the purest water I can get, then the same water with sugar, then with salt. If only the salt water makes many bubbles, the ions from the salt carry the electricity.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing at a time and includes plain water as the comparison. It says what result would show the idea is wrong.

items.p: A doorbell button by the sea rings by itself on misty mornings. Explain why, using ions.
items.a: Sea wind leaves salt on the button. Mist wets the salt, and its ions become free to move. They carry a small current between the two contacts, as a finger on the button would.
items.why: A strong answer says why the dry salt did nothing at noon. The ions were there all day, but they could not move.

items.p: In Powder Detective, lemon juice made bubbles, though it has no metal atoms. What does this show?
items.a: Some covalent molecules split into ions in water. So the guide from the kinds of atoms is a first guess, and a test is needed to check it.
items.why: A strong answer keeps the guide and marks its limit. It does not throw the guide away because of one exception.

items.p: Steel is harder to bend than pure iron. Use the idea of sliding layers to explain why.
items.a: Steel has other atoms mixed in among the iron atoms. Atoms of a different size get in the way, so the layers cannot slide as easily.
items.why: A strong answer links bending to layers of atoms sliding, and says what the added atoms do to the sliding.

items.p: Is a chemical bond a real thing?

views.says: Yes. A bond has a length and a strength that we can measure. A microscope picture shows lines where the bonds are.
Only nuclei and electrons are real. 'Bond' is our name for a place where electrons gather.
The line is a drawing. It is useful, because it predicts what materials will do.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about bonds. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that salt has no single lines to draw, yet it is held very strongly. Another is that bond lengths can be measured.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer says what would count as evidence for a bond being a thing.

items.p: Draw what happens when salt dissolves. Show one sodium ion and the water molecules around it.
items.a: A sodium ion marked plus, away from the lattice, with several water molecules around it. The oxygen end of each water molecule points towards the ion.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the ion still charged and separate, with water molecules turned the right way round.
items.art: A corner of a lattice of plus and minus circles on the left and empty space on the right.

quiz.p: How does an atom become a plus ion?
quiz.why: Electrons are minus. An atom that loses one has more plus charge than minus. If you chose gains, that makes a minus ion.

quiz.p: What holds the ions in salt together?
quiz.why: Each plus ion attracts every minus ion near it. Shared pairs make covalent bonds, and a pool of electrons makes a metallic bond.

quiz.p: Which pair of atoms will share electrons?
quiz.why: Hydrogen and oxygen are both non-metals, so neither gives an electron away. A metal with a non-metal makes ions, and two metals pool their electrons.

quiz.p: Which of these is made of molecules?
quiz.why: Sugar is carbon, hydrogen and oxygen joined by covalent bonds. Salt is a lattice of ions, and copper and brass are metals.

quiz.p: Why does a metal shine and carry electricity?
opts: It has ions in a lattice
quiz.why: Free electrons flow as a current, and they send light back from the surface.

quiz.p: Salt melts on a kitchen flame.
quiz.why: False. Salt melts at about 800 degrees Celsius, because every ion is held strongly on all sides.

opts: When it is dissolved or melted
quiz.why: Dissolving and melting both free the ions. Free ions can move, and moving charges carry electricity.

quiz.p: A solid flattens when pressed and carries electricity when dry. What is it?
quiz.why: Only a metal does both. An ionic solid cracks and carries electricity only when wet or melted.

quiz.p: Magnesium is a metal and oxygen is a non-metal. Which bond joins them?
quiz.why: The metal atom gives electrons to the non-metal atom. Magnesium oxide is made of ions.

quiz.p: What kind of evidence showed that salt has no molecules?
opts: The pattern X-rays make in a crystal
quiz.why: X-rays bounce off the layers of ions and make a pattern of spots. The pattern shows every ion with six equal neighbours.

quiz.p: Most real bonds are partly shared and partly given.
quiz.why: True. Pure sharing and full giving are the two ends of a line, and most bonds lie between them.
Each water molecule has a slightly plus end and a slightly minus end. Many of them together pull an ion out of the lattice.

applications: A tank-full alarm has two metal probes near the top of a water tank. When the water reaches them, the ions in the water carry a small current and a buzzer sounds.
Electricity companies near the sea wash salt off the insulators on their power lines. Damp salt would let electricity leak across them.
A phone battery works by moving lithium ions through a liquid from one side to the other. The electrons go round through the phone.
ORS holds sodium and potassium salts. In water they split into ions, which the body needs for nerves and muscles to work.
Copper and aluminium are pulled into wires, because metals stretch without breaking. Their free electrons carry the current.
Dorothy Hodgkin used X-rays to find where every atom sits in penicillin and in insulin. Knowing the shape of a medicine's molecule helps chemists make it.

open_questions.q: Is a chemical bond a real object, or a useful way of drawing where electrons are?
open_questions.why_open: Bond lengths and strengths can be measured, and microscopes show lines between atoms. But quantum theory describes only nuclei and electrons, and chemists disagree about what to call real.

open_questions.q: Can solid metallic hydrogen be made and kept?
open_questions.why_open: It was reported in 2017, but nobody has repeated it. The pressure needed is close to the limit of what diamond tools can stand.

open_questions.q: What is the hydrogen deep inside Jupiter and Saturn like?
open_questions.why_open: Models say it is a liquid metal. No probe has gone that deep, and laboratories can hold such pressures only for a moment.

open_questions.q: Can we predict how a new material will behave just from its atoms?
open_questions.why_open: For simple crystals, computers do this well. For large molecules and mixtures, the calculations are still too big, and surprises are common.

open_questions.q: Can a metal be made that carries electricity with no loss at room temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Some materials do this when very cold or under huge pressure. Scientists do not fully understand why, so they cannot yet design one for everyday use.

Which things on this table would bend if you pressed them, and which would break?
Why is the handle of a pressure cooker made of plastic, and the body of metal?
The spoon in the hot sambar feels hot. What carried the heat up the handle?
Your sweat tastes salty. What does that tell you about the water inside your body?
Why does the salt in the dabba go lumpy in the rainy season?
A gold bangle can be bent open, but a glass bangle breaks. What might be different inside them?
If wet hands are dangerous near a switch, what in the water is carrying the electricity?

jokes.j: What did one oxygen atom say to the other?
Why do metal atoms make good team players?
Why did the salt crystal give up yoga?

jokes.j: What did the wet salt say to the dry salt?

Why did the wax leave the heating test first?

maths.problem: In Slide a Row, a flat square of 16 coins has 8 plus ions and 8 minus ions. A cube of salt has 4 layers like this. How many ions does it have, and how many are sodium?
maths.explain: One layer has 4 times 4, which is 16 ions. Four layers have 4 times 16, which is 64. Plus and minus take turns in every direction, so half are sodium. Half of 64 is 32.
maths.context: In Slide a Row you build a flat model of a salt crystal from 16 coins. A real crystal has many such layers.
maths.why_maths: A crystal repeats one pattern in three directions. Multiplying counts the ions without drawing them all.

maths.problem: In Give and Take, an aluminium card gives 3 electrons and an oxygen card takes 2. What is the smallest set in which the electrons given equal the electrons taken?
maths.explain: The electrons given must be a multiple of 3. The electrons taken must be a multiple of 2. The smallest number that is both is 6. Two aluminiums give 6, and three oxygens take 6.
maths.context: In the card game Give and Take, metal cards give electrons and non-metal cards take them. A set is complete when both totals are equal.
maths.why_maths: The formula of an ionic compound comes from the smallest number that both atoms' electrons divide into.

maths.problem: Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius, candle wax at 60, aluminium at 660 and salt at 800. Suppose a spoon over a candle reaches 300 degrees. Which of the four melt in the spoon? How much hotter must it get to melt salt?
maths.answer: Ice and wax melt. The spoon must get 500 degrees hotter to melt salt.
maths.explain: 0 and 60 are below 300, so ice and wax melt. 660 and 800 are above 300, so aluminium and salt stay solid. 800 minus 300 is 500.
maths.context: In Three Solids, Three Tests a grown-up heats salt, wax and foil in a spoon over a candle. The wax melts, and the salt and the foil stay solid.
maths.why_maths: Comparing each melting point with the spoon's temperature predicts the result before the test.

maths.problem: One gram of gold can be beaten into leaf that covers about 5,000 square centimetres. A square leaf is 10 centimetres long and 10 centimetres wide. How many such leaves does one gram make?
maths.explain: One leaf covers 10 times 10, which is 100 square centimetres. 5,000 divided by 100 is 50.
maths.context: In Three Solids, Three Tests a ball of aluminium foil flattened under a spoon and did not break. Gold flattens even further.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the whole area by the area of one leaf shows how far a metal can spread without breaking.

maths.problem: In Powder Detective, a child predicted 6 results from the kinds of atoms. The guide was right for salt, cooking soda, sugar and glucose. It was wrong for lemon juice and vinegar. What fraction did the guide get right? Is the guide still worth using?
maths.answer: 4 out of 6, which is two thirds. Yes, as a first guess that a test must check.
maths.explain: 4 right out of 6 is the fraction four sixths. Dividing both numbers by 2 gives two thirds. A guide that is right two times in three is useful. The two misses are both acids, so they show where the guide needs care.
maths.context: In the project Powder Detective you predict which kitchen things carry electricity in water. Then you test them with the bubble tester.
maths.why_maths: A fraction says how far a rule of thumb can be trusted. Looking at what the misses share shows where the rule fails.

maths.problem: A grain of table salt is a tiny cube. About 1 million ions sit in a line along one edge. About how many ions are on one flat face of the grain?
maths.explain: A face is a square with 1 million ions along each side. 1 million times 1 million is 1 million million. That is 1 followed by 12 zeros.
maths.context: In Slide a Row you lay 4 rows of 4 coins as a model of salt. A real grain of salt has about a million ions along each edge.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the ions along two edges shows how many particles even one face of a single grain holds.
