how_we_found_out.story: Before 1913, chemists were sure that salt was made of molecules. Each molecule was thought to be one sodium atom joined to one chlorine atom. In 1912 William Bragg and his son Lawrence, in England, began to shine X-rays through crystals. The rays bounced off the layers of atoms and made a pattern of spots on a photographic plate. From the spots, the two men could work out where the atoms sat. In 1913 Lawrence, aged 23, worked out the pattern of salt. There were no pairs at all. Sodium and chlorine sat in turns, like the squares of a chessboard. Each had six of the other kind around it. Many chemists disliked this. In 1927 the well-known chemist Henry Armstrong wrote to the journal Nature. He called the chessboard idea 'repugnant to common sense'. But every later measurement agreed with the Braggs. In 1915 father and son shared the Nobel Prize in Physics. Lawrence was 25, and nobody younger has won that prize.
how_we_found_out.who: William Bragg and his son Lawrence Bragg in England, and the chemist Henry Armstrong, who objected
how_we_found_out.when: The Braggs began in 1912. Lawrence Bragg published the structure of salt in 1913. They shared the Nobel Prize in 1915. Armstrong's letter appeared in 1927.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That salt is made of separate molecules, each with one sodium atom and one chlorine atom. X-ray patterns showed a lattice in which every ion has six equal neighbours and no partner of its own.
how_we_found_out.art: A young man in the clothes of 1913 holding a photographic plate covered in a regular pattern of dark spots, with a cube-shaped model of balls and rods on the bench beside him.

roots.context: In this unit you found three ways that atoms hold on to each other. Here we ask what salt, water and metal tell us about what a thing is.

deep_truth.truth: In Dry Salt, Wet Salt, dry salt carried no electricity. The same salt carried it once water was added, and water alone carried almost none. So the charged ions were in the dry salt all along, each held in place by its neighbours. Whether salt carries electricity depends on whether its ions are free to move.
deep_truth.habit: We sort materials into conductors and insulators, as if each label were fixed inside the material. Salt is an insulator when dry and a conductor when wet. The label describes how the particles are held at that moment.
deep_truth.evidence: In Dry Salt, Wet Salt, the same two teaspoons of salt gave no bubbles dry and many bubbles wet. Plain water and wet sugar gave almost none. In Slide a Row, every ion in the coin model was held on all sides.

three.who_am_i: Your nerves and muscles work by ions moving through water. Sodium ions from the salt you eat are part of how you move your hand.
three.what_is_life: A living body uses every kind of bond at once. Covalent chains make its flesh, ionic crystals make its bones and shells, and free ions carry its messages.
three.what_is_this_world: A salt pan, a river and a copper mine are built from the same kinds of particles. They differ in where the outer electrons sit.

roots.thread: Every bond in this unit is the same attraction, between plus charges and minus electrons. Salt, water and copper differ only in where the outer electrons end up. They are given, or shared by two atoms, or shared by all. From that one attraction come hardness, melting, shine and the signals in your nerves. Many sages taught that the many things of the world come from one source. The science here says something close and plain: thousands of materials come from one attraction, arranged in different ways.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to put salt in water overnight. In the morning the salt cannot be found, yet every sip of the water is salty.
teachings.link: The salt has not gone. Its ions have left the lattice and spread through the water. The Upanishad uses this as a picture of the self present in everything, which science does not test.

teachings.teaching: Whatever arises in dependence on other things has no fixed nature of its own.
teachings.link: Salt does not carry electricity by its own nature, and water hardly does. Together they do. What salt can do depends on what it is with.

teachings.teaching: A statement about a thing is true 'in some respect'. From one side a thing is so, and from another side it is otherwise.
teachings.link: Is salt a conductor? When wet, yes. When dry, no. The Jain teachers asked us to state the condition along with the claim, as a careful scientist does.

science.text: Every chemical bond comes from one force, the electric attraction between nuclei and electrons. Quantum theory has been used to calculate bonds since 1927.
Chemists and philosophers argue about whether a bond is a real object. The other view is that it is a useful drawing of where electrons are.

other_view.view: Words such as 'gives', 'shares' and 'holds on' are only figures of speech. Charges attract each other by the electric force, and electrons settle where the energy is lowest. On this view, wet salt carrying electricity is an ordinary fact of physics. It says nothing deeper about what a thing is.

practice.title: One grain on the tongue
practice.say: Hold a steel spoon in one hand and one grain of salt in the other. Feel how hard each one is. Now put the grain on your tongue and close your eyes. Notice the moment the taste begins. The ions are leaving the crystal and moving into the water of your mouth. Sit quietly for five breaths while the taste spreads.
practice.kid: Hold a spoon and a grain of salt. Feel how hard they are. Put the grain on your tongue. Close your eyes. Notice when the taste begins. Breathe five times.

ask: In Dry Salt, Wet Salt, the same salt was an insulator and then a conductor. Which one is salt really?
A grain of salt has no pairs, and a copper wire shares its electrons among all its atoms. Where does one piece of salt or copper end?
The sodium in salt was once a metal that burns in water. Is it still the same thing now?

playtest: Every experiment, activity and game was reasoned through step by step against its materials list. None of them was tried in a kitchen. Bend or Break and Three Solids, Three Tests need crystal salt, a candle, foil and old spoons. Salt cracks best as a big crystal. With fine salt, press a pinch between two spoons. Over a candle, wax melts in about 15 seconds, and salt and foil stay solid. A hot salt grain can crack and jump, so heat only about ten grains and keep faces away. Dry Salt, Wet Salt needs a 9-volt battery with a snap clip, which most families must buy. The tester gives fine bubbles at both pencil tips within seconds when the probes touch. The saucers and cups must not be metal, or the tester bubbles all the time. Tap water and borewell water hold some salts, so plain water and wet sugar may give a few slow bubbles. Count that as 'few'. Salt goes damp in the monsoon and may then give a few bubbles when 'dry'. Warm it in a dry pan first. The wet salt test is kept to a count of 20, in an airy room. Electricity in salt water can make a trace of chlorine. In Powder Detective, lemon juice and vinegar are meant to surprise. Vinegar may give only a few bubbles. In the Tank-Full Alarm, the tank must be glass or plastic, and the bubbles are slow, so use a torch. Slide a Row works with any 16 coins. Give and Take can be finished alone with no card left over. Facts to treat with care: the melting points are rounded. A spoon over a candle is taken to reach a few hundred degrees, which was not measured. The million ions along the edge of a salt grain is for a grain about 0.3 millimetres wide. Liquid metallic hydrogen inside Jupiter comes from models and brief laboratory tests. The Upanishad, Nagarjuna and Jain teachings are given as paraphrases. The three videos have no address yet.
